title: Connection Pooling
description: Master database connection pool sizing with the HikariCP formula, HTTP keep-alive mechanics, connection leak detection, and PgBouncer deployment patterns.

segments.text: A database connection is expensive. TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, authentication, session setup — all told, roughly 20 to 50 milliseconds. If you open and close a connection for every query, you're burning time and exhausting database resources. Connection pooling is one of the most impactful optimizations in production.

A connection pool maintains a set of pre-established database connections. When your application needs a connection, it borrows one from the pool. When done, it returns it. No handshake, no teardown. HikariCP, the gold standard for JVM connection pools, can acquire a connection in under one microsecond from a warm pool.

Pool sizing is where most teams get it wrong. The HikariCP formula: optimal pool size equals the number of CPU cores times two, plus the number of spinning disks. For a typical 8-core server with SSDs, that's roughly 16 to 20 connections. More connections actually decrease throughput because of context switching and lock contention on the database.

Think about this counterintuitive result. A team increased their pool from 20 to 200 connections to handle more traffic. Database CPU went to 100 percent, query latency tripled. They reduced back to 20 and latency dropped. Why would more connections make things slower?
segments.thought_prompt: Why does increasing connection pool size past a threshold actually decrease database throughput?

segments.text: With 200 connections, the database has 200 sessions competing for the same locks, buffer pool pages, and CPU cores. Each connection holds memory for its session state, typically one to ten megabytes in PostgreSQL. 200 connections means two gigabytes just for session overhead. Lock contention grows quadratically with connection count.

PgBouncer sits between your application and PostgreSQL as a lightweight connection proxy. In transaction pooling mode, it multiplexes thousands of application connections onto a small pool of real database connections. A common production setup: 500 application connections funneled through PgBouncer into 30 real PostgreSQL connections.

PgBouncer in transaction mode has gotchas. Prepared statements break because they're bound to the real connection. Session-level settings like SET statement_timeout get lost between transactions. LISTEN/NOTIFY doesn't work. You must use session pooling mode for these features, which limits multiplexing.

Connection leaks are silent killers. A code path that borrows a connection but never returns it due to an unhandled exception. The pool slowly drains until all connections are exhausted and new requests block. HikariCP detects this with leak detection threshold: if a connection isn't returned within 30 seconds, it logs a stack trace of the borrower.

HTTP keep-alive is connection pooling at the HTTP layer. Instead of opening a new TCP connection for each request, the connection stays open for multiple requests. HTTP/1.1 made this default. Without it, every request pays the TCP handshake cost of one round trip, plus TLS negotiation. Nginx defaults to keeping 75-second idle connections.

A production incident: after a deployment, a service started timing out. Investigation revealed the connection pool was exhausted. The new code path opened a transaction, called an external API that took five seconds, then committed. Five-second transactions holding connections meant the pool of 20 was constantly full.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you redesign this code path to avoid holding a database connection during an external API call?

segments.text: Monitor these pool metrics: active connections, idle connections, pending requests waiting for a connection, and connection acquisition time. Alert when pending requests exceed zero for more than 30 seconds. In Prometheus, HikariCP exposes hikaricp_connections_active and hikaricp_connections_pending gauges.

Connection pooling is simple in concept, subtle in practice. Size your pools small and measure. Use PgBouncer when you have more application instances than your database can handle. Always set leak detection thresholds. And never hold a database connection while waiting on an external call.
